evidence.title: Advice quality and observed reliance differ from responses to an AI label
evidence.observation: Source-reported finding: Gaube and colleagues report an online eight-case chest-X-ray experiment with radiologists and other physicians. All advice was human-authored but labeled either AI or experienced radiologist. Diagnostic accuracy was lower with inaccurate advice, without a significant purported-source effect. Experts rated AI-labeled advice less favorably, but that attitude did not prevent susceptibility; some participants rejected every inaccurate recommendation. Observation context: Recruitment/experiment dates not established from inspected text.

source_locations.SRC-150: Results: Diagnostic accuracy and advice quality; Discussion limitations; Methods: Participants and study design; Table 3

evidence.limitations: Simulated cases, no actual AI output or patient outcomes, and no unassisted baseline: this does not demonstrate AI-caused clinical harm. Prose reports 138 radiologists and 127 other physicians, while Table 3 totals 264; that internal denominator discrepancy remains unresolved. Experience skew and few incorrect-advice cases restrict generalization.
evidence.open_questions: Which results transfer to other populations, tool versions, longer periods and operational governance settings? No such transfer is established by inclusion.
evidence.support_assessment: Commons interpretation: Expressed attitudes and observed reliance can differ. Expert participation alone did not ensure rejection of incorrect advice.

terms.name: Meaningful human control
terms.definition: A condition in which people retain adequate information, independent judgment, authority, and practical means to redirect consequential activity. A nominal human-in-the-loop approval does not, by itself, demonstrate this capacity.

terms.name: Operational trust
terms.definition: Reliance placed in an AI-enabled capability through actual use, decisions, and delegation, whether or not users express subjective confidence in it. Trust in this sense is operational behavior, not a reliability certification.
